newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reforms tenders in anti-corruption move.
newsitem.headline: France reforms tenders in anti-corruption move.

text.p: France's centre-right government announced on Thursday plans for sweeping changes to the awarding of public works contracts in a move to clamp down on corruption.
The changes are the first major overhaul in 59 years of the public procurement system which has been at the centre of many of France's most explosive political scandals in recent yars.
The changes "are essential as much for our economy as for the good functioning of our democracy", Industry Minister Yves Galland told a news conference.

The proposed legislation, tightening supervision of the awarding of contracts and vastly simplifying procedures and regulations, will be debated this spring in parliament and is expected to come into effect by year end.

Corruption would be "rigorously pursued in a context of absolute transparency," Galland said. The changes were "essential to end the climate of permanent suspicion which surrounds the public works market".

All of the country's major political parties as well as many prominent politicians have been tainted by allegations of taking kickbacks from corporations in exchange for awarding public works contracts.
Dozens of businessmen and some of France's biggest blue chip corporations have been investigated over sleaze allegations.
A law was passed in 1990 tightening rules on party funding but the legislation failed to stop the eruption of scandals.

President Jacques Chirac, whose own Gaullist RPR party has been hit by corruption probes into links between party funding and public works contracts, praised the legislation at a cabinet meeting, saying it paved the way for greater openness.
Under the new public works code, public works commissions will now include members from all political parties and will be involved in the awarding of all contracts.
The commissions will be asked to give an opinion on the awarding of all bids under 700,000 francs and will choose the winner for all contracts of 700,000 francs or more.
The changes also move away from automatically awarding contracts to the lowest bidder, instead focusing on the "best buy".

Galland said public authorities had tended in the past to buy the cheapest without regard to quality. "Many public buildings have photocopiers which were the cheapest but turned out to need more expensive paper or elevators that were the least expensive but needed more expensive maintenance," he said.
Any bid that appeared to be abnormally low would be investigated, he added, for possible abuse of competition.
The code's language, which "had become incomprehensible" will also be simplified, Galland added.
